body_en:
Plenty of data looks stable on the surface, but everyone knows how the economy really feels.

Yasheng Huang, a professor at MIT, has laid out eight of the clearest, most grounded judgments on the economy today — blunt, direct, no detours, no whitewash. Once you hear them, the whole economic picture clicks into place.

1. Jobs and Income Are the Real Ballast of Stability

What truly determines social stability and ordinary people's lives is never a pretty GDP growth rate — it's jobs and household income.

No matter how good the economic data looks, if people's wallets aren't growing with it, that growth is hollow. It has no real substance for people's livelihoods.

2. Weak Consumption Is a Disease of Income

Consumption stays sluggish across the market, and the root cause isn't that people don't want to spend — it's that incomes have been stagnant for a long time.

Consumption's share of GDP has long sat at the bottom among major economies, around 40%. Every consumption stimulus treats the symptom, not the cause.

The real test of the economy is whether lower- and middle-income people actually have money to spend.

3. The Private Economy Is the Ballast of Social Stability

The private economy is, without question, the ballast of social stability.

When private firms are thriving, there are more jobs, more chances for ordinary people to move up, and social tensions get buffered as much as possible.

A stable private sector means stable livelihoods.

4. We Don't Lack Technology — We Lack Commercialization

We have never lacked technology or innovation. Our biggest shortcoming is the ability to turn innovation into money.

We hold an enormous number of patents, and technical breakthroughs keep coming — but vast amounts of research stay on paper, never becoming industry, never creating jobs, never turning into real income for ordinary people.

5. The Other Side of Cheap Convenience Is Low Income

All the cheap convenience we enjoy is, at its core, ordinary people's low income.

Food delivery in minutes, parcels the next day, a ride-hailing car whenever you want it. Behind that extreme convenience are countless manual workers putting in extremely long hours for extremely low pay.

A low-cost economy is, from another angle, cheap labor.

6. Only Two Paths Ahead

The economy has only two paths ahead. There is no third.

Either an L-shaped adjustment — shifting gears, slowing down, consolidating the base, stabilizing the fundamentals — or a stepwise decline, where every slide is propped up by stimulus, the underlying problems never get fixed, and the risks only keep piling up.

7. Flooding the System Won't Break the Deadlock

Short-term flooding — pumping up the numbers with investment — can only prop up the data briefly. It cannot break the deadlock.

For the economy to truly break through, the only way out is sustained, deepening reform. Institutional breakthroughs are the lasting cure.

8. We Won't Repeat Japan's Lost Thirty Years

We won't repeat Japan's lost thirty years. Our per-capita GDP still has room to grow, our entrepreneurs are still energetic, and capital keeps flowing in.

But all of that rests on one precondition: the direction of development must not reverse, and the pace of reform must not stop.

Conclusion

These eight judgments aren't pleasant to hear, but every one of them is grounded.

The economy's biggest problem was never the fluctuation of the data — it's the structural rot underneath. Facing the problems squarely, instead of numbing ourselves, is the only way forward.
excerpt_en: The headline numbers look steady, but everyone knows how the economy actually feels. MIT professor Yasheng Huang lays out eight blunt, grounded judgments — no spin, no sugarcoating.
title_en: Yasheng Huang: Eight Core Judgments on the Economy Today
